id: I'm a Fool to Love You

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Some, About, She

outputs.L1:
Some folks will tell you the blues is a woman,  
Some kind of supernatural creature.

My mother would tell you, if she could,  
About her life with my father,  
A strange and sometimes cruel gentleman.  
She would tell you about the choices  
A young Black woman faces.

Is falling in love with a man  
A deal with the devil?  
In blues terms—the tongue we use  
When we don’t want nuance  
To get in the way,  
When we need to talk straight—

My mother chooses my father  
After choosing a man  
Who was, as we sing it,  
Of no account.

This man made my father look good—  
That’s how bad it was.  
He made my father seem like an island  
In the middle of a stormy sea.  
He made my father look like a rock.

And is the blues the moment you realize  
You exist in a stacked deck?  
You look in a mirror at your young face—  
The face my sister carries—  
And know it is the only leverage  
You’ve got.

Does this create a hurt that whispers,  
“How you going to do?”

Is the blues the moment  
You shrug your shoulders  
And agree: a girl without money  
Is nothing, dust  
To be pushed around by any old breeze?

Compared with this,  
My father seems, briefly,  
To be a fire escape.

This is the way the blues works  
Its sorry wonders:  
Makes trouble look like  
A feather bed,  
Makes the wrong man’s kisses  
A healing.
outputs.L2:
People sometimes describe the blues as female,  
as an otherworldly being.  
If my mother were here to speak,  
she might recount her years with my father—  
an unusual man, at times unkind—  
and explain the limited paths  
open to a young Black woman.

She might ask whether loving a man  
is another kind of bargain with evil.  
That is how the blues would put it:  
in the blunt language we turn to  
when subtlety becomes an obstacle  
and only the plain truth will do.

Before my father, my mother picked someone  
who, as the old songs say, was worthless.  
He was so terrible that beside him  
my father appeared dependable—  
an island amid violent waters,  
something solid enough to cling to.

Perhaps the blues begins when you understand  
the game has been fixed against you.  
You study your youthful reflection,  
the same face my sister now wears,  
and recognize that your beauty  
is the sole advantage available to you.

Maybe that knowledge produces an ache  
that quietly asks, What will you do now?  
Perhaps the blues arrives when you give in,  
lifting your shoulders and accepting  
that a penniless girl counts for nothing—  
mere dust carried wherever  
an ordinary gust decides to take it.

Against such bleak possibilities,  
my father could briefly resemble  
an emergency exit.  
This is the blues performing  
its mournful illusions:  
turning danger into comfort,  
making hardship feel soft as a bed,  
and transforming the kisses of the wrong man  
into something that seems capable of healing.
outputs.L3:
The speaker uses the blues as a metaphor for the painful choices and harsh realities that shape the life of a young Black woman. The mother’s decisions are not presented as freely made; instead, they are constrained by poverty, racism, gender inequality, and her need for safety. After being treated so badly by a previous man, she chooses the speaker’s father because, by comparison, he seems stable and protective. His appeal comes less from genuine security than from the fact that her earlier experiences have lowered her expectations of what safety and love can look like.

The poem also suggests that beauty may seem like one of the few forms of power available to a young woman when social and economic forces are working against her. The mother uses that beauty as leverage, hoping it can provide affection, protection, or an escape from powerlessness. Yet the father offers only a temporary refuge. Although he is strange and sometimes cruel, she initially interprets his attention as a form of rescue because her alternatives appear even worse.

In this way, the blues both expresses and distorts suffering. It transforms danger into something that resembles comfort and makes the affection of the wrong man feel healing. The mother’s relationship with the father reflects the tragic logic created by hardship: when pain is familiar and genuine safety seems unreachable, even an unstable or harmful love can appear to be salvation.
outputs.L4:
The poem draws on the language, mood, and imagery of the blues to portray a young Black woman’s struggle for love and security in a society shaped by poverty, racism, and gender inequality. The speaker reflects on her mother’s choices not simply as personal mistakes, but as responses to a world that offers her few safe or hopeful possibilities. Material hardship limits her independence, racism narrows her social and economic opportunities, and patriarchal expectations make attachment to a man seem necessary for protection and stability. Her search for affection is therefore inseparable from her need to survive.

Within these conditions, even a cruel, unreliable, or unsuitable man can appear to offer refuge. The mother’s willingness to accept such a relationship reveals the force of desperation: when the alternatives are loneliness, poverty, and vulnerability, limited protection may seem better than none at all. The poem does not romanticize this choice, but it also refuses to reduce the woman to weakness or poor judgment. Instead, it invites readers to understand the social pressures that shape her decisions. What appears to be an individual failure is exposed as the result of a deeply unequal system.

The blues is especially important because it gives form to suffering without allowing suffering to have the final word. Its sorrowful rhythms and images express disappointment, longing, and betrayal, while the act of voicing those experiences becomes a form of endurance. Through the blues, pain is transformed into testimony: the speaker can name the forces that have wounded her family and preserve the emotional truth of her mother’s life. The poem ultimately presents the blues as a language of survival within a social order stacked against Black women—a way to mourn constrained choices, recognize the conditions behind them, and continue speaking despite hardship.
outputs.L5: She wanted to learn more about the world, so she packed some clothes, a notebook, and a camera. Although she felt nervous, she was excited about the journey ahead. Along the way, she met kind people, discovered beautiful places, and learned some valuable lessons about courage, friendship, and herself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem exploring the idea that “the blues is a woman,” focusing on a Black mother’s difficult romantic choices and the limited options imposed by poverty and sexism.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Blues Is a Woman**

The blues is a woman  
counting rent money twice  
at the kitchen table,  
though the number will not grow.

She has three children asleep  
behind a curtain,  
their dreams warm as loaves  
she cannot afford to waste.

A man comes home carrying roses  
and the smell of somebody else.  
Another promises steady work,  
but his hands turn hard after payday.  
A third has tenderness enough  
and no place to live.

Do not ask her  
why she stays,  
why she leaves,  
why she returns.

Ask the landlord  
why mercy costs extra.  
Ask the factory gate  
why it closes at five  
when school lets out at three.  
Ask the law why a woman’s fear  
must arrive bruised  
before it is believed.

The blues is a woman  
choosing between doors  
built by men  
who kept the keys.

She loves, yes—  
not foolishly,  
but with the fierce arithmetic  
of hunger:

this man’s paycheck  
against that man’s rage,  
one night’s shelter  
against a lifetime of apology,  
a father for the children  
against the child he becomes.

In the morning  
she oils her daughter’s scalp,  
parts the dark hair clean,  
makes two bright roads  
through the country of the head.

Be better than what found me,  
her fingers say.  
Be freer than my choices.

Then she stands,  
puts on her good shoes,  
and carries the whole blue morning  
under her coat—

not singing because sorrow is pretty,  
but because breath  
must become something  
before it breaks.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a narrative poem in which the speaker reflects on why her mother chose a cruel father after being mistreated by an even worse man.
counterfactuals.output:
**The House She Chose**

Before my father, there was one  
whose name my mother kept  
behind her teeth,  
a splinter she would not let us see.

He taught her doors could lock from both sides,  
that roses might arrive apologizing  
for the hand that snapped the vase,  
that love could kneel in broken glass  
and still demand forgiveness.

When she escaped, she carried little:  
a coat, a photograph,  
the habit of listening for footsteps,  
the belief that any room without a fist  
was almost heaven.

Then came my father—  
not gentle, but gentler.  
He did not strike where bruises showed.  
He rationed kindness like winter bread,  
called silence peace,  
called jealousy devotion,  
called her lucky.

As a child, I watched her smooth  
the tablecloth after thunder,  
set his dinner by the clock,  
lower her voice until it fit  
inside the life he gave her.

Why him? I asked the dark.  
Why leave a burning house  
to live beside a smoking one?  
Why praise the man who only  
sometimes lit the match?

Years later, she told me—  
not in confession,  
but while peeling apples,  
the red skins falling in one long coil:

*When you have lived beneath a boot,*  
*an open hand looks holy.*  
*When the worst has named itself love,*  
*you learn to measure mercy*  
*by how much pain is spared.*

I wanted to be angry.  
Perhaps I was.  
But there she stood, small knife shining,  
making sweetness from what she could,  
cutting rot away in careful circles.

I saw then what choice had meant:  
not a road beneath clear weather,  
not two bright doors,  
but one wolf and another  
farther off, his teeth less red.

She chose the cruelty  
she had been taught to recognize,  
the cage with wider bars,  
the man who let her sometimes sing  
and never asked why singing  
sounded so much like fear.

Mother, I do not call it love.  
I will not bless the harm  
because it harmed you less.

But now I know  
the heart can mistake survival  
for desire,  
and a woman fleeing night  
may choose the first dim room  
that promises not to be darkness.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a blues-inspired poem about a young Black woman who sees marriage as a temporary escape from hardship, using imagery such as a stacked deck, a stormy sea, and a fire escape.
counterfactuals.output:
**Borrowed Door**

She was a young Black woman with the rent due twice,  
Lord, the rent due twice,  
Life dealt a stacked deck and called the cheating nice.  

He came with a gold ring, said, *Baby, take my name,*  
A warm room for the winter, a shelter from the rain—  
But she knew some wedding vows were just another borrowed flame.  

She said, *Marriage ain’t heaven; it’s a fire escape,*  
A narrow iron ladder from the hunger and the scrape.  
*I’ll rest above the smoke awhile, then choose my own shape.*  

Her heart was a stormy sea beneath a moonless sky,  
Love was one small lifeboat that might not keep her dry.  
Still, she climbed in singing—too proud to drown, too tired to die.  

So deal that stacked deck, dealer; she has learned to mark the cards.  
Let the stormy sea rise angry, let the night come down hard.  
She’ll leave that fire escape someday  
and build a house with her own yard.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a raw, conversational poem about how desperation can make a dangerous man seem safe and the wrong man’s affection feel healing?
counterfactuals.output:
I knew he was dangerous.

Not movie dangerous—  
no leather jacket, no warning music—  
just the kind that makes you rehearse  
simple questions before asking them.

But I was tired.  
God, I was tired.

And when you’ve been drowning long enough,  
you stop asking why the hand  
reaching for you  
is wearing brass knuckles.

He called me beautiful  
like he was returning something  
the world had stolen.

He listened—  
or stayed quiet in the right places.  
Back then, I couldn’t tell the difference.

I mistook being wanted  
for being known.  
Mistook his jealousy for shelter,  
his grip for gravity,  
the way he needed me afraid  
for the way love says,  
*please don’t go.*

That’s the ugly truth:

desperation can turn a locked door  
into a home.

It can make a wolf look warm  
because at least  
he has fur.

And the wrong man’s affection—  
when you have gone untouched  
in all the places that matter—  
can feel medicinal.

Even when the bottle says poison.  
Even when your hands shake  
every time you reach for it.

I thought I was healing  
because the pain had changed.

That’s all.

It had changed its voice,  
learned my name,  
started kissing me afterward.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a literary free-verse meditation that asks whether the blues begins when a woman realizes her beauty is her only leverage in an unjust world.
counterfactuals.output:
**First Note**

Does the blues begin  
the morning a woman understands  
the mirror is not a witness  
but a marketplace—

that the world has weighed her face  
before hearing her name,  
has priced the bright animal of her body  
and called the price power?

Perhaps it begins earlier:

in the hand withdrawn from the ledger,  
the schoolhouse door closing,  
the wage thinned to a thread,  
the law turning its marble head  
while hunger learns her address.

Then beauty enters  
in its red dress,  
carrying a key that fits  
only certain locks,  
only for a season.

She may open one door with it,  
and behind that door  
find another man holding the hinge.

Is that the first blue note—  
not that she is beautiful,  
but that beauty is the lone coin  
the unjust world agrees to recognize?

Listen:

even the coin is borrowed.  
Even the face in the glass  
is told how long it may shine.  
Even desire, when used as a ladder,  
leans against somebody else’s wall.

Still, she adorns herself.

Not always for them.  
Sometimes lipstick is a small flag  
raised over the country of her mouth.  
Sometimes the hips move  
because the body remembers  
a freedom no law invented.

And perhaps the blues begins there too—  
where sorrow refuses to surrender rhythm,  
where a woman turns the measure  
meant to measure her  
into music.

She sings:

I am more than what opens the door.  
I am the room.  
I am the road beyond it.  
I am the hand, the key,  
the lock broken clean.

And the world, unjust and listening,  
cannot tell whether she is mourning  
or warning it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
